body: A man who drives a van for a living hears the same song four times before two o’clock. Once at the depot with the shutter up and his hands full. Once on the bypass. Once outside a house in a cul-de-sac where nobody is in, while he writes the card. And once more between the fourth drop and his lunch, and this time he sings the chorus, all of it, with the window down. He does not like the song. If you stopped the van and asked him he would tell you he thinks it is thin, and that the words do not mean much. He would also be able to sing you the second verse.

Both of those things are true at once, and the gap between them is the whole subject. Nothing about him has been persuaded. Something has simply been installed, by a route that has nothing to do with whether he agrees.

Commercial music radio runs on repetition. The strongest tracks sit in heavy rotation, which in practice means several plays a day, and the reason is well understood in the trade: the best predictor of whether somebody says they like a song is how often they have already heard it.

It is worth being exact about what repetition does, because it is not persuasion. A song you have never heard is a stranger, and the first hearing is spent mostly on orientation — where the chorus is, whether there is a key change, what sort of thing this is. By the fourth hearing none of that work is left to do, and the ease of that is experienced from the inside as pleasure. You are not enjoying the song more. You are enjoying the absence of effort, and there is no way to tell those two apart while it is happening. Repetition does not argue with you. It moves a song from unfamiliar to familiar, and then leaves you to interpret the familiarity as consent.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. The flagship holds one rule that costs more than any other on the band: within a single day it will not play you the same song twice.

That rule is expensive. A day of unrepeated music needs a catalogue several times larger than a day of rotation, and every hour of it has to be worth airing. It gives up the retention that familiarity buys, and familiarity is the cheapest listener loyalty there is. Nobody would choose this if the object were to build a hit. Repetition is how you build a hit, and familiarity is not the same thing as agreement — and on a station carrying the words of the faith, that difference matters more than the audience figures.

Because the mechanism does not know it has changed subject. It works exactly as well on a worship song as on a soft drink jingle. A chorus can be installed in a congregation by rotation alone: played into a church because it is played on the radio, sung on Sunday because it was played in church, and beloved within a season without a single person having weighed what it says. The affection that accumulates is indistinguishable, from the inside, from agreement. People end up defending a line they have never once examined, and they are not being dishonest: there is no felt difference to tell.

So the flagship is built the other way round. The day is scheduled ahead and published before it airs, the pool it draws from is rebuilt whenever new music lands, and no title comes round twice between one midnight and the next. Two people tuning to the same number at the same second hear the same song, which is what makes it a broadcast rather than a feed. None of that is clever. It is a constraint held to, and constraints held to are what distinguish a station from a playlist with a name on it.
The obvious objection is a good one, and it should be met head on.

Repetition is how a congregation learns to sing at all. Nobody has ever sung a song they heard once. The hymns that carried people through the last century were sung weekly for decades, and their words went in so deep that they surfaced at gravesides sixty years later. That is repetition doing the best work it has ever done. But notice what governed it. A congregation chose those hymns, over years, in daylight. Heavy rotation is a different animal wearing the same coat: it is repetition at a tempo nobody chose, decided in an office, on a scale of hours rather than years, and applied to whatever is currently being promoted. The first is a body learning its own songs. The second is saturation with a schedule attached.
A song you have heard four hundred times is not a song you have agreed with. It is a song you can no longer hear.

A woman is typing up the order of service on a Thursday evening, because it has to be at the printer by nine. She has sung the second song in it every few weeks for three years, and she can hear the tune while she types. Set out as text, without the tune underneath it, the second line says something she does not think is true. Not heresy — nothing anybody would stand up about. Just a sentence that quietly makes God owe her an outcome, phrased smoothly enough that in three years of singing it with her eyes shut she has never had one thought about it. She types it in anyway, because it is Thursday and the printer closes at nine. But she sits and looks at it for a while first.

Nothing had gone wrong in that church. The tune had simply been carrying the sentence past her, forty or fifty times. Rotation is how the line got in. Nothing else about the song had to be true for it to work.

The cost of refusing to repeat is real. You will hear something you love in the morning and it will not come back that day. You cannot use the flagship to learn a new song, which is a genuine loss for a family wanting to sing one at home: learning needs repetition, and this station has given that away. That is not a small complaint and there is no answer to it except that the trade was made knowingly.

But the missing second play is not a hole in the service. It is the service. A song that gets one hearing has to be good on one hearing; it cannot borrow authority from having been round three times already. It has to stand on what it says, in the three minutes it has, to a listener who has never met it. That is a far harder test than heavy rotation ever sets, and it is the only one that leaves the listener still able to notice what they are being asked to sing.

There is a second dividend. Heavy rotation implies a small pool, and a small pool means that almost everything which is not the current handful never airs — most of what is old, most of what is unusual, and most of what came from anywhere other than the few places that presently export worship music to the world. Refusing to repeat forces the catalogue open. The week gets wider by arithmetic rather than by good intentions, which is the only way a week has ever got wider.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel and much else. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: clean, entertaining, and playable in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, 40 of them across 29 languages, hosted in their own tongues rather than translated into them afterwards.

The station this article has been describing is HM 308.70 — Year of Jubilee, the flagship of the band. It carries continuous worship and teaching from the Inspire Family catalog, day and night, and it will not play you the same song twice in a day. That single rule is the reason to start there rather than anywhere else. It is the station you can leave on for eight hours in a kitchen or a workshop without the day narrowing to six songs, and it is the one that will not quietly recruit your affection for a lyric by wearing you down with it. You will not love every track, and you are not meant to. You will, however, still be able to hear the ones you do — which is the thing rotation takes first, and takes so gently that nobody notices it going.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 308.70 on for a whole working day, and at the end of it try to name the song you heard most. You will not be able to, because there was not one. Then notice what you can name: probably two or three you had never heard before and could describe the words of. That is what a day sounds like when nothing has been repeated at you, and it is very difficult to go back afterwards.
